title: The Brothers Karamazov
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
openingChapterLabel: Book I, Chapter 1 — Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov
openingText: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a land owner well known in our district in his own day, and still remembered among us owing to his gloomy and tragic death, which happened thirteen years ago, and which I shall describe in its proper place. For the present I will only say that this “landowner”—for so we used to call him, although he hardly spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange type, yet one pretty frequently to be met with, a type abject and vicious and at the same time senseless. But he was one of those senseless persons who are very well capable of looking after their worldly affairs, and, apparently, after nothing else.
about:
The Brothers Karamazov is the story of a father and his three sons in a small Russian town. The father is a buffoon and a sensualist; the sons are a soldier, an intellectual, and a novice monk. They argue, love the same woman, and live through their father's murder and its aftermath. Around this family Dostoevsky builds his largest novel — debates about God, suffering, freedom, and the meaning of love.

Dostoevsky was 58 when he finished it, and he died three months after publication. It was meant as the first of two novels; the second was never written. What we have is already 800 pages, including the most famous chapters in his work — "Rebellion," "The Grand Inquisitor," and the encounters between Alyosha and the dying elder Zosima. It is the most argumentative novel ever written and the closest Dostoevsky came to answering the questions he had been asking since Notes from Underground.

angleCards.title: Faith vs. doubt.
angleCards.text: Ivan cannot accept a God who permits children to suffer. Alyosha cannot accept a world without God. Their conversation in the tavern is the sharpest collision between these two positions in all of literature. Neither wins.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the debate between Ivan’s reasoned rebellion against God and Alyosha’s faith—and see whether Dostoevsky thinks either of them can answer the other.

angleCards.title: The Grand Inquisitor.
angleCards.text: Ivan’s prose poem imagines Christ returning to 15th-century Seville, only to be arrested by the Church. The Inquisitor explains, calmly, why humanity cannot bear freedom and must be ruled. It is one of the most disturbing arguments ever written—and Dostoevsky believed the only answer to it was not an argument.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Brothers Karamazov as the context for the Grand Inquisitor: to understand what provokes it, what Alyosha’s silent kiss means, and what Dostoevsky thought the reply to it was.

angleCards.title: Three brothers as three paths.
angleCards.text: Dmitri is passion—desire, guilt, and redemption. Ivan is reason—brilliant, proud, and ultimately unable to live inside his own conclusions. Alyosha is faith—not naïve, but tested and chosen. Dostoevsky built them to stand for three ways of being human. Watch which one the novel endorses.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read each brother as a distinct mode of being—passion, reason, faith—and see what Dostoevsky thinks each one can and cannot do.

angleCards.title: Zosima’s alternative.
angleCards.text: The elder Zosima teaches something radically different from Ivan’s rebellion: that everyone is responsible to everyone, that love is not a feeling but a practice, and that the world’s suffering is met not by argument but by presence. His chapters are Dostoevsky’s answer to the Grand Inquisitor.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Zosima’s teaching as Dostoevsky’s counter-argument to Ivan—and see whether ‘active love’ is a real reply to the problem of suffering or simply a change of subject.

cast.name: Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov
cast.description: A drunk, lecherous, shameless buffoon who somehow made a fortune. He abandoned all three of his sons in childhood, and when the novel opens, he is competing with his eldest son over the same woman. He is comic, repulsive, and oddly human—the wound the whole family carries.

cast.name: Dmitri Karamazov
cast.description: A former soldier, chronically in debt, violent in passion, and convinced his father has cheated him of his inheritance. He loves two women at once and cannot choose between them. He is the most obviously guilty person in the room—which is exactly why the novel is not straightforward.

cast.name: Ivan Karamazov
cast.description: The second brother, brilliant and ice-cold. He has built a philosophy that can justify anything and believes in nothing—or says he does. His argument against God is the sharpest in the novel, but the novel is quietly testing whether a man can actually live inside it.

cast.name: Alyosha Karamazov
cast.description: The youngest brother and the novel’s moral centre. He is a novice at the monastery, devoted to the elder Zosima, and constitutionally incapable of judging anyone. Where Ivan argues, Alyosha simply loves—and Dostoevsky treats that as the harder and more radical act.

cast.name: Father Zosima
cast.description: The revered monk and Alyosha’s teacher. He teaches that each person is responsible for everyone and for everything, and that active love—not pity, not sentiment—is the only real reply to suffering. His life and his teachings form the novel’s spiritual counterweight to Ivan.

cast.name: Smerdyakov
cast.description: The illegitimate son of Fyodor Pavlovitch, raised as a servant in his own father’s house. Pale, sullen, and contemptuous of everyone. He has read Ivan’s philosophy carefully—and unlike Ivan, he takes it to its logical conclusion.

acclaim.quote: The Brothers Karamazov is the most magnificent novel ever written.
The three books I read every year are The Old Testament, Moby-Dick, and Brothers Karamazov.
acclaim.context: interview, The Paris Review, The Art of Fiction No. 12, 1956

whyItMatters.title: The Argument About God
whyItMatters.body: Ivan's "Rebellion" chapter and "The Grand Inquisitor" make the strongest case against God ever put in a novel. Alyosha and Zosima do not refute the argument intellectually. The novel asks whether love can do what reason cannot.

whyItMatters.title: The Father Question
whyItMatters.body: The Karamazov father is a man almost no one would defend, and yet he is the father. The novel deals with what we owe to people who do not deserve it — to family, to authority, to God when God seems indefensible. It is the deepest treatment of the question in literature.

whyItMatters.title: Everything in One Book
whyItMatters.body: Dostoevsky tries to put everything he knows into this book — politics, faith, sex, money, crime, death, the meaning of suffering, whether children deserve their pain. It does not all hold together neatly. That is part of what makes it the book it is.
